title: Ars Notoria sive Flores Aurei
shelf_note: No tradition or collection is set, so there is no shelf to test. The leaf is a two-column Gothic Latin manuscript of the Ars Notoria: a prayer, the fifth oration of nomina barbara, then prologues. That agrees with the title and the medieval date.
rights_flag: The scan carries a licence mark burned into the image: a diagonal watermark "ALL RIGHTS RESERVED © Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana" across the text, and a footer bar "Copyright © Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana / powered by AMLAD·NTT DATA". The work itself is a medieval manuscript, but the image is under the holding library's reuse terms.
structure_note: The structure counts give pages_translated 0, but the book field says 70 translated, and this page has a translation. The instrument count is wrong (E2). Only 19 of 72 pages have a printed number and there are 5 backsteps. On a manuscript with faint, sparse foliation (on this leaf only a faint "4" at the top right), these are more likely misread folio or margin numerals than real disorder. A strip of the facing leaf shows at the left edge, and the OCR correctly ignored it.

pages.layout: two columns of Gothic textualis with red rubrics; the edge of the facing leaf visible at left; Vatican watermark across the text

ocr_errors.image: Incipit prolog' posterior orationis quinte (red rubric at the top of column b)
ocr_errors.problem: The rubric is misread as the heading that actually comes further down the column. A reader is told that the second prologue of the fifth prayer opens the sixth hour, so the section structure of the work is wrong.

ocr_errors.ocr: Christe almi creator pceptoz mīific mĩroz op-
ocr_errors.image: [L]egifer altissime preceptor mirifice ... optime (the initial is left blank for a rubricator)
ocr_errors.problem: The prayer is addressed to the 'most high Lawgiver'. The OCR makes it an address to Christ ('Christe almi creator'), which is not on the leaf.

ocr_errors.ocr: Ad adorationū tuorum & dñi lonez misericor-
ocr_errors.image: Ad cogitationum sermonum & operum bonorum institutor / & amator ...
ocr_errors.problem: The opening line of the prologue is misread ('author and lover of good thoughts, words [and works]' becomes 'adorations ... merciful'). The whole column b prologue is heavily garbled from here on.

ocr_errors.image: auctor adesto queso dñe supplicationibus meis & aperi ...
ocr_errors.problem: 'adesto queso ... supplicationibus' ('be present, I pray, to my supplications') is misread, and the translation then invents a different petition from it.

ocr_errors.ocr: mentis pscuant ut parte per te & in te mi uiuātus
ocr_errors.image: mens pseuerant ut per te p[ro] te & in te illuminatus
ocr_errors.problem: 'illuminatus' is misread as 'mi uiuātus', and the translation renders it as 'living'.

ocr_errors.ocr: regno eternitatis regis maiestatis tue in gloriam
ocr_errors.image: regno eternitatis atque maiestatis tue ad gloriam

tr_errors.english: ### Here begins the prologue of the first prayer of the sixth hour
tr_errors.problem: This carries the OCR misread of the rubric 'posterior prologue of the fifth prayer'. The English now prints the same heading twice in a row, the second time correctly, and attaches the fifth prayer's prologue to the sixth hour.

tr_errors.source: Christe almi creator pceptoz mīific mĩroz op-
tr_errors.english: Christ, kindly Creator, wonderful teacher of wonders, best
tr_errors.problem: The leaf has 'Legifer altissime' (most high Lawgiver). The English invents an address to Christ, with no unclear marker.

tr_errors.english: I beg you, Lord, <unclear>do not look upon</unclear> my sins,
tr_errors.problem: The source asks the Lord to be present to 'my supplications' and to open his eyes. The English invents a petition not to look on 'my sins'. It is marked unclear, but it is still a fabricated sense.

tr_errors.source: Ad adorationū tuorum & dñi lonez misericor-
tr_errors.english: <unclear>To the worship</unclear> of your <unclear>holy ones</unclear>, O good Lord, lover of the merciful,
tr_errors.problem: This is built on the garbled OCR. The source has 'author and lover of good thoughts, words and works'.

tr_errors.source: mentis pscuant ut parte per te & in te mi uiuātus
tr_errors.english: so that through you and in you, living,
tr_errors.problem: The source has 'illuminatus' (enlightened), and that word matters in a prayer for knowledge.

other.note: Because of the misread rubric, the reader sees the same heading 'Here begins the prologue of the first prayer of the sixth hour' printed twice in succession.
The OCR carries a <warning> block (describing the bleed-through and the Vatican stamp) inside the transcription.

missing.english: Here begins the fifth prayer, which is of the sacred particles
missing.why: The English never explains that the following block is a string of nomina barbara (magical names), recited and not meant to be understood. The meta only says it is 'not translatable'.

missing.english: Here begins the prologue of the first prayer of the sixth hour
missing.why: A general reader needs to know that the Ars Notoria arranges its prayers by numbered orations and set hours of recitation.

missing.english: who shut and no one opens, who open and
missing.why: This is a quotation of Revelation 3:7 (the key of David) that the reader is not told about.

missing.english: into whom the angels long to
missing.why: This is an allusion to 1 Peter 1:12, and the sentence leans on it.

book_verdict: This is the right leaf of a genuine Ars Notoria manuscript. Column a's prayer is read and translated passably. The column b prologues are heavily garbled, and the translation builds on them: a misread rubric attaches the fifth prayer's prologue to the sixth hour, and an address to 'Christ' is invented where the leaf reads 'Legifer'. The scan also carries a Vatican 'All rights reserved' watermark.
